newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. sanctions body seeks details of Libyan flights.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sanctions body seeks details of Libyan flights.

text.p: The U.N. Libya sanctions committee asked its chairman on Thursday to obtain further information about an alleged violation of sanctions last week by Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.
A flotilla of four Libyan aircraft was reported to have flown Gaddafi and others to Niger and Nigeria, in defiance of a U.N. air embargo against Libya over the Lockerbie affair.
The Security Council decided on Tuesday to ask its Libya sanctions committee to establish the facts.

The committee's chairman, Ambassador Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland, told reporters after Thursday's closed-door session that he had been requested to "get in touch with the ambassadors of states concerned to get more details" in preparation for another meeting on Monday.

Other sources said most members of the 15-nation committee were satisfied that sanctions had been breached but that China and Egypt wanted to be certain that the planes had in fact taken off from Libya.

The Libyan news agency said at the time that Gaddafi visited the West African countries to hold prayers marking the Moslem new year as head of the Islamic Popular Leadership, an organisation he created in 1989.

Libya has been subject to mandatory U.N. sanctions since 1992, including a ban on international flights and an arms embargo, for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States in the 1988 mid-air bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.

The United States had intended showing the sanctions committee television news footage about last week's flights and another alleged Libyan sanctions violation, and a television set was set up in the committee room.

But a committee source said that before the meeting got under way, France, joined by Egypt, China and Russia, complained that advance notice should have been given of the intended display and its relevance explained.

The planned screening was not discussed during the meeting and in the end the footage was not shown. It was said to include shots not only of last week's Libyan flights but of the August 1996 crash soon after takeoff from Belgrade of a chartered Russian Ilyushin-76 transport plane that, according to news reports at the time, was carrying ammunition and aircraft parts bound for Libya via Malta.
